prior.title: Read element symbols
prior.reminder: An element symbol identifies an element. Upper- and lower-case letters matter: Co is cobalt, while CO is carbon monoxide.

steps.prompt: How many different elements are in H₂O?
steps.hint: Read the symbols H and O.
steps.working: H is hydrogen and O is oxygen: two elements.

steps.prompt: How many different elements are in CO₂?
steps.hint: Read C and O; the small 2 is not another element.
steps.working: Carbon and oxygen are two elements.

prior.title: Count atoms in a formula
prior.reminder: A subscript applies to the symbol immediately before it. No subscript means one.

steps.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in one H₂O molecule?
steps.hint: Read the small number after H.

steps.prompt: How many atoms in total are in one H₂O molecule?
steps.hint: Add the hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

prior.title: Count groups and molecules
prior.reminder: A number outside brackets multiplies everything inside. A coefficient multiplies the whole formula.

steps.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are represented by Ca(OH)₂?
steps.hint: There are two OH groups.
steps.working: Each OH has one O; two groups contain two O atoms.

steps.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are represented by 3H₂O?
steps.hint: Each water molecule contains two H atoms.

prior.title: Positive and negative charges
prior.reminder: A proton has charge +1 and an electron −1. Add the charges to find the net charge.

steps.prompt: A particle has 3 protons and 3 electrons. Find its net charge.
steps.hint: Calculate 3 − 3.

steps.prompt: A particle has 3 protons and 2 electrons. Find its net charge.
steps.hint: Calculate 3 − 2.
steps.working: Net charge +1. Losing an electron makes a particle more positive.

prior.title: Recognise states of matter
prior.reminder: (s) means solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) dissolved in water.

steps.prompt: What state does (g) represent? Enter one word.
steps.hint: Use the first letter as a clue.

steps.prompt: Does (aq) mean dissolved in water or melted? Enter dissolved or melted.
steps.hint: Aqueous means a solution in water.
steps.working: (aq) means dissolved in water; it is not the same as a pure liquid.

prior.title: Separate physical and chemical changes
prior.reminder: In a physical change the substances keep their chemical identities. A chemical change produces different substances.

steps.prompt: Ice melts into liquid water. Enter physical or chemical.
steps.hint: Both ice and liquid water are H₂O.
steps.working: This is a physical change: the state changes, not the chemical identity.

steps.prompt: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Enter physical or chemical.
steps.hint: Magnesium oxide is a new substance.

prior.title: Convert mass units
prior.reminder: 1 g = 1000 mg. Write the unit before choosing a conversion.

steps.prompt: Convert 2 g to mg.
steps.hint: Multiply by 1000.

steps.prompt: Convert 500 mg to g.
steps.hint: Divide by 1000.

prior.title: Convert solution volumes
prior.reminder: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ and 1 cm³ = 1 mL. Mole calculations often need volume in dm³.

steps.prompt: Convert 250 cm³ to dm³.
steps.hint: Divide by 1000.

steps.prompt: Convert 0.50 dm³ to cm³.
steps.hint: Multiply by 1000.

prior.title: Use a ratio
prior.reminder: In a 1:2 ratio, the second amount is twice the first.

steps.prompt: A model uses one A particle for every two B particles. How many B are needed for 3 A?
steps.hint: Multiply 3 by 2.

steps.prompt: If 4 B are available, how many A can react with them?
steps.hint: Divide 4 by 2.

prior.title: Use powers of ten
prior.reminder: 10³ means 1000. Scientific notation keeps very large or small numbers manageable.

steps.prompt: Calculate 2 × 10³.
steps.hint: Multiply 2 by 1000.

steps.prompt: Write 0.004 as a × 10⁻³. Find a.

prior.title: Substitute into a formula
prior.reminder: Write the formula, substitute values with units, then calculate.

steps.prompt: Use density = mass ÷ volume. Mass is 12 g and volume is 3 cm³. Find density in g cm⁻³.
steps.hint: Divide 12 by 3.

steps.prompt: Use mass = density × volume. Density is 4 g cm⁻³ and volume is 5 cm³. Find mass in g.
steps.hint: Multiply 4 by 5.

prior.title: Calculate a change and a percentage
prior.reminder: Change = final − initial. A percentage means a number out of 100.

steps.prompt: Temperature rises from 20 °C to 27 °C. Find the temperature change in °C.
steps.hint: Subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature.
steps.working: 27 − 20 = 7 °C. The temperature change is also 7 K.

steps.prompt: A sample is 25% salt by mass. Find the salt mass in a 20 g sample.

sections.title: Particles and mixtures
sections.reminder: An element contains one type of atom. A compound contains different elements chemically bonded; a mixture contains different substances together.

steps.prompt: A sample contains only O₂ molecules. How many types of atom are present?
steps.hint: Both atoms in O₂ are oxygen.
steps.working: Only one type of atom: oxygen. O₂ is an element, even though each molecule has two atoms.

steps.prompt: Salt and sand are mixed together. Enter mixture or compound.
steps.hint: Mixing does not automatically create new chemical bonds.
steps.working: Salt and sand form a mixture; each substance retains its identity.

sections.title: Count subatomic particles
sections.reminder: Atomic number Z counts protons. Mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

steps.prompt: A carbon atom has atomic number 6 and mass number 12. How many protons does it have?
steps.hint: The atomic number is the proton count.

steps.prompt: How many neutrons does that carbon atom have?
steps.hint: Calculate mass number minus atomic number.

sections.title: Place a few electrons
sections.reminder: For these first-ten-element examples, the first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8. This simple shell model is a starting point for orbital configurations.

steps.prompt: A neutral lithium atom has 3 electrons. Put 2 in its first shell. How many remain?
steps.hint: Subtract the two placed electrons from the total.

steps.prompt: A neutral neon atom has 10 electrons. How many are in its second shell?
steps.hint: Put 2 in the first shell, then count what remains.
steps.working: 10 − 2 = 8. Neon has a full second shell.

sections.title: Mass to moles
sections.reminder: Amount n = mass m ÷ molar mass M. M is measured in g mol⁻¹; n is measured in mol.

steps.prompt: Water has molar mass 18 g mol⁻¹. Find the amount in 18 g, in mol.
Find the amount in 36 g of water, in mol.
steps.hint: Use the same molar mass.

sections.title: Temperature and gas volume
sections.reminder: Gas-law temperatures must be in kelvin: T/K = temperature/°C + 273.15. At constant pressure and amount, ideal-gas volume is proportional to kelvin temperature.

steps.prompt: Convert 0 °C to K.
An ideal gas has volume 2 dm³ at 300 K. At constant pressure and amount, find its volume at 600 K in dm³.
steps.hint: The kelvin temperature doubles, so the volume doubles.

sections.title: Balance ionic charges
sections.reminder: An ionic formula has zero net charge. Use the smallest whole-number ratio of positive and negative ions.

steps.prompt: One Na⁺ and one Cl⁻ have what total charge?
steps.hint: Add +1 and −1.

steps.prompt: How many Cl⁻ ions balance one Mg²⁺ ion?
steps.hint: Each chloride ion contributes −1.
steps.working: Two Cl⁻ supply −2, balancing +2. The formula is MgCl₂.

sections.title: Share an electron pair
sections.reminder: A single covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. A double bond contains two shared pairs.

steps.prompt: How many electrons are in one shared pair?
steps.hint: A pair contains two items.

steps.prompt: How many shared electrons are in a double bond?
steps.hint: There are two pairs.

sections.title: Explain a metal simply
sections.reminder: Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized electrons. These electrons can move through the solid.

steps.prompt: Which particles carry charge through a solid metal: electrons or protons?
steps.hint: Look for particles that are free to move through the structure.
steps.working: Delocalized electrons carry charge through the solid metal; protons remain in nuclei.

steps.prompt: Are the metal ions in this model positive or negative?
steps.hint: They have contributed electrons to the delocalized system.

sections.title: From units to materials
sections.reminder: An alloy combines a metal with other elements. A polymer contains many linked repeating units.

steps.prompt: Brass contains copper and zinc. Enter alloy or pure element.
steps.hint: There is more than one element in this metallic material.

steps.prompt: A short addition-polymer model has 5 repeat units, each containing 2 carbon atoms. How many carbon atoms are represented?
steps.hint: Multiply units by carbons per unit.

sections.title: Read rows and columns
sections.reminder: Periodic-table periods are horizontal rows and groups are vertical columns. Sodium is in period 3, group 1.

steps.prompt: Which period contains sodium?
steps.hint: Use the row number stated above.

steps.prompt: A neutral sodium atom has shell arrangement 2,8,1. How many electrons are in its outer shell?
steps.hint: Read the final number.
steps.working: There is 1 outer-shell electron, consistent with group 1.

sections.title: Read a simple organic formula
sections.reminder: Carbon usually makes four covalent bonds in these neutral molecules. An alcohol contains an –OH group attached to a saturated carbon.

steps.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in CH₃CH₂OH?
steps.hint: Count the two C symbols.

steps.prompt: CH₃CH₂OH contains an –OH group. Enter alcohol or alkane.
steps.hint: Use the functional group described above.

sections.title: Measure a temperature rise
sections.reminder: For water warming up, q = mcΔT gives energy gained by the water. In the simple insulated model, the reaction loses that energy.

steps.prompt: Water warms from 20 °C to 25 °C. Find ΔT in K.
steps.hint: A temperature difference has the same numerical value in °C and K.

steps.prompt: Use m = 10 g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT = 5 K. Find q for the water in J.
steps.hint: Multiply 10 × 4.18 × 5.
steps.working: q = 209 J gained by the water.

sections.title: Read an energy change
sections.reminder: Reaction enthalpy change = product enthalpy − reactant enthalpy. A negative value means an exothermic reaction.

steps.prompt: Reactants are at 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and products at 30 kJ mol⁻¹ on a relative energy scale. Find ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹.
steps.hint: Subtract 80 from 30.

steps.prompt: Is this change exothermic or endothermic?
steps.hint: A negative ΔH means energy is released to the surroundings.
steps.working: It is exothermic; the products are lower in enthalpy.

sections.title: Energy per gram of fuel
sections.reminder: Energy per gram = energy released ÷ mass of fuel. Compare like units and the same conditions.

steps.prompt: A fictional fuel releases 60 kJ when 3 g burns. Find its energy release per gram in kJ g⁻¹.
steps.hint: Divide 60 by 3.

steps.prompt: At the same release per gram, how much energy would 2 g release in kJ?
steps.hint: Multiply 20 kJ g⁻¹ by 2 g.

sections.title: Start Gibbs energy (AHL)
sections.reminder: AHL starter: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Use kelvin and matching energy units. A negative ΔG indicates thermodynamic favourability under the stated conditions, not a fast reaction.

steps.prompt: Convert ΔS = 100 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ to kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps.hint: Divide by 1000.

steps.prompt: With ΔH = 20 kJ mol⁻¹, T = 300 K and ΔS = 0.100 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹.
steps.working: 20 − 30 = −10 kJ mol⁻¹; thermodynamically favourable under these conditions.

sections.title: Read a balanced equation
sections.reminder: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the coefficients show particle or mole ratios. Balance by changing coefficients, not chemical formulas.

steps.prompt: How many H atoms are represented by 2H₂?
steps.hint: Two molecules, each containing two hydrogen atoms.

steps.prompt: With oxygen in excess, how many mol of H₂O form from 2 mol H₂?
steps.hint: The H₂:H₂O mole ratio is 2:2.

sections.title: Calculate an average rate
sections.reminder: Average rate of gas production = change in gas volume ÷ time interval.

steps.prompt: Gas volume increases from 10 to 30 cm³. Find the increase in cm³.
steps.hint: Final volume minus initial volume.

steps.prompt: This increase takes 5 s. Find the average rate in cm³ s⁻¹.
steps.hint: Divide the increase by the time.

sections.title: Recognise dynamic equilibrium
sections.reminder: At dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, forward and reverse rates are equal. Reactions continue and concentrations stay constant; the concentrations need not be equal.

steps.prompt: At equilibrium the forward rate is 3 mmol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Find the reverse rate in the same units.
steps.hint: The two rates are equal at equilibrium.
steps.working: The reverse rate is also 3 mmol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

steps.prompt: At equilibrium, do the reactions continue or stop?
steps.hint: Dynamic means that both directions are still occurring.
steps.working: Both reactions continue at equal rates.

sections.title: Transfer a proton
sections.reminder: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one.

steps.prompt: In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, how many protons does each HCl donate?
steps.hint: Compare HCl with Cl⁻.

steps.prompt: Water accepts that proton. Is it acting as an acid or a base?
steps.hint: Accepting a proton is the role of a base.
steps.working: Water is acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

sections.title: Transfer electrons
sections.reminder: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.

steps.prompt: Complete the electron count: Mg → Mg²⁺ + __ e⁻.
steps.hint: Balance the +2 charge with negative electrons.

steps.prompt: Magnesium loses electrons. Enter oxidation or reduction.
steps.hint: Use oxidation = loss.

sections.title: Split a bond equally
sections.reminder: In homolytic bond breaking, each atom receives one electron from the shared pair. A radical has an unpaired electron.

steps.prompt: A Cl–Cl bond breaks homolytically. How many bonding electrons does each Cl receive?
steps.hint: Share the two bonding electrons equally.
steps.working: Each chlorine atom receives one electron from the bond.

steps.prompt: How many chlorine radicals form from one Cl₂ molecule?
steps.hint: Each of the two chlorine atoms becomes a radical.

sections.title: Donate an electron pair
sections.reminder: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre. In a mechanism, a full curly arrow shows movement of a pair.

steps.prompt: How many electrons are represented by one full curly arrow?
steps.hint: A full curly arrow moves one pair, not one electron.
steps.working: A full curly arrow represents movement of 2 electrons.

steps.prompt: Does a nucleophile donate or accept an electron pair?
steps.hint: Use the definition above.
steps.working: A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts it.
